articles.title: US Envoys See Ukraine Peace Progress As NATO Debate Resurfaces
articles.summary: But Russia cast doubt on that assertion and talks involving Ukrainian and Western officials in Berlin left major questions unresolved
articles.body: WASHINGTON -- US and European officials have edged closer to unity on a Ukraine peace framework, with Washington open to NATO-style security guarantees and US envoy Jared Kushner saying Moscow may be receptive to the idea. But Russia cast doubt on that assertion and talks involving Ukrainian and Western officials in Berlin left major questions unresolved, including how Ukraine would be protected against another Russian attack, whether its territorial integrity would be preserved, and what concessions might be required for a settlement. As European leaders push for a role in peace negotiations alongside the US, Ukraine, and Russia, US envoy Steve Witkoff said “important work remains.” Witkoff, who attended the Berlin meeting on November 19 along with Kushner, President Donald Trump's son-in-law, described the discussions as “frank and productive.” He said Trump was determined to end the war in a way that preserves Ukraine's security and sovereignty and prevents a recurrence of conflict. The meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, a group of countries coordinating military and other support for Ukraine, was hosted by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and attended by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and other leaders. It sought to strengthen Western support for Kyiv and secure a European role in US-led peace efforts. Kushner offered an indication of the US administration's thinking on Ukraine's postwar security, saying Washington had made progress in securing Russian acceptance of the idea of an Article 5-style guarantee -- a commitment modeled on NATO's collective-defense clause, under which an attack on one member is considered an attack on all. “From America's perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal,” he said, adding that Trump was open to the idea, provided it served US interests and formed part of a broader security package. Kushner said Washington had made Moscow “comfortable” with the concept, arguing that Russia also wanted to avoid another war after the current conflict. He acknowledged, however, that skepticism remained about Moscow's intentions. Russia, which wants any peace deal to include a bar on Ukraine ever joining NATO, threw cold water on the idea that Moscow might accept an arrangement that included Article 5-like guarantees for Ukraine. "I want to say that even finding a formula for 'quasi-membership' in NATO for Kyiv -- or seeking some sort of, in quotation marks, 'creative solution' in this area -- is an unacceptable option for us," Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said on November 20. Kyiv and the West "should acknowledge the nonnegotiable nature of our demand that [Ukraine] must not join NATO," the Russian news agency Interfax quoted Ryabkov as saying. "Once that happens, I believe the question of security guarantees could, in one way or another, be discussed." Pentagon Official Says Ukraine War Likely To Last Through Winter, Despite Mediation Efforts An Article 5-like guarantee could replicate elements of NATO's collective-defense commitment without making Ukraine a member of the alliance. Its credibility would depend on the legal obligations, military arrangements, and the willingness of participating countries to respond to another Russian attack. Zelenskyy said Ukraine would like more clarity on what such a guarantee would involve. "I'm not sure that we have a common [understanding] of Article 5," he said, adding that for him, it means "that there some forces of partners on your land" and suggesting that in his view, US and European forces should be based in Ukraine. Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron urged Ukraine's allies to reconsider NATO membership rather than rely exclusively on alternative security arrangements. “Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine's accession to NATO,” Macron said. Macron also called for urgent deliveries of air-defense systems and interceptors to protect Ukrainian civilians and critical infrastructure from Russian missile and drone attacks. A joint statement following the Berlin meeting by the leaders of Germany, France, Britain, and Ukraine reaffirmed that Kyiv must receive robust, legally binding security guarantees once a cease-fire takes effect. The proposed framework could include sustained military, financial and technical assistance, participation in a US-led cease-fire monitoring mechanism and a European-led multinational force supported by Washington. Wider Europe Briefing: Europe's Fruitless Search For A Ukraine Peace Envoy; EU Safeguards For Montenegro The force could provide reassurance measures on land, at sea and in the air while helping consolidate Ukraine's armed forces. The leaders also envisaged a legally binding commitment, subject to national procedures, to take measures to restore peace and security if Russia attacks again. Moscow vocally opposes Western troop deployments in Ukraine as part of security guarantees, a position President Vladimir Putin repeated this week. The joint statement stressed that Ukraine's sovereignty, territorial integrity and right to choose its security arrangements must be respected. It also rejected changing international borders by force. The coalition pledged continued military and financial support for Kyiv and increased economic pressure on Moscow, including measures targeting Russian energy revenues, cryptocurrency transactions, illicit financial flows, and its military-industrial complex. The European leaders also called for an energy cease-fire during the winter and an arrangement to protect food exports through the Black Sea, as Russian attacks threaten Ukraine's power supplies and the war continues to disrupt maritime trade. Putin Has Shown No Willingness To End Ukraine War, Says Mike Pompeo Merz said further peace negotiations were expected soon, with Europe participating alongside the US, Russia, and Ukraine. He suggested the United Arab Emirates as a possible neutral venue. Kushner said Trump wanted an agreement developed with European and Ukrainian participation, not imposed unilaterally by Washington. “President Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side,” he said. The diplomatic efforts are unfolding amid growing criticism in Washington of Trump's recent engagement with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Trump met Putin and Xi at an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, on November 19, which produced no breakthrough on ending Russia's war in Ukraine. A joint US-Chinese-Russian statement made no mention of the war. The senior Democrat in the US Senate, Chuck Schumer, dismissed the trilateral meeting as a diplomatic embarrassment, arguing that Trump had secured no meaningful commitments on Ukraine or international security. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Senate Democrat on foreign policy, said defeating Putin in Ukraine remained essential to US national security. Trump, Xi, And Putin Make History, But No Breakthroughs: 4 Takeaways From The Trilateral Summit Representative Gregory Meeks, the senior Democrat on the Foreign Affairs Committee in the House of Representatives, said the summit had not advanced nuclear nonproliferation, ended Russia's war, or addressed Chinese human rights abuses. Republican Senator Thom Tillis also questioned the intentions of Moscow and Beijing, while Representative Don Bacon criticized Trump's approach, saying Republicans had traditionally stood up to Russia and China. Democratic Senator Tim Kaine introduced a resolution seeking answers from the administration about purchases of Russian fuel, sanctions relief, and delays in delivering air-defense munitions to Ukraine. He argued that buying Russian fuel risked providing Moscow with revenue to finance its war.

articles.title: Kushner says Russia is 'comfortable' with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end war after Trump talks with Putin
articles.body: BERLIN (AP) — U.S. envoy Jared Kushner on Thursday said Russia is "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end the war as it nears the five-year mark. Another American envoy, Steve Witkoff, said U.S. President Donald Trump discussed Ukraine and a peaceful end to the war during his trilateral talks with the Russian and Chinese leaders earlier Thursday. Kushner and Witkoff met with European allies in Berlin to discuss their support for Ukraine after a third Ukrainian aerial attack in four days on the key Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Russian-held Crimea halted rail traffic across the span, officials said Thursday, after earlier strikes shut down the road section of the landmark that is a symbol of Moscow's invasion. Train traffic across the bridge stopped after the overnight strike while authorities assessed the damage, but it resumed in the afternoon, according to Russian state news agency RIA Novosti. The Ukrainian strikes seemed calculated to embarrass Russian President Vladimir Putin as he met in China with President Xi Jinping and Trump, as well as to demonstrate that Kyiv still holds cards in the war and to undermine Russia's argument that its victory is inevitable. The attack came hours before the start of talks in Berlin between Kushner, Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alongside more than 40 European leaders who are supporting Ukraine's war effort and fear being sidelined by Trump's direct talks with Putin. The American leader called into the Berlin talks following his meeting with Putin, Kushner said. "We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that," Putin told reporters in Shenzhen, China. He insisted the bridge is a civilian asset, adding that he had ordered the bridge closed to the transport of military hardware or ammunition. Putin also said that the road side of the bridge had been "seriously damaged" but vowed to rebuild it. The rail section is believed to be stronger than the road side, to bear the greater weight of cargo wagons. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The 19-kilometer (12-mile) Kerch Bridge is a key route for military and civilian supplies to Crimea, which Moscow seized in defiance of international law in 2014 and uses to support front-line troops. It is a potent reminder of Russia's illegal annexation of the territory and has been a prime target for Ukraine. A large section of the road deck and an arch collapsed in the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes over seven stages of the operation, according to Zelenskyy, and the train track was damaged by domestically produced Neptune missiles, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said. Now Russia will need to reroute fuel and ammunition supplies over land, where "our drones are waiting for the cargo," the ministry said. The Russian Defense Ministry said Thursday that its air defenses intercepted 53 Ukrainian drones over 10 Russian regions during the night. A Ukrainian attack on Russia's Saratov region killed three people and wounded two others, local Gov. Roman Busargin said, and a drone killed a woman traveling by bicycle with her 8-year-old grandson in the Bryansk region, Gov. Egor Kovalchuk said. Ukrainian authorities said that Russia launched anti-ship missiles and 98 drones at Ukraine, with hits recorded at 18 locations. Explosions and sirens rang out across Kyiv during the day, and the Dutch and Austrian embassies sustained minor damage, officials said. Two people, including a 44-year-old woman, were killed and at least 23 people, including a 12-year-old boy, were reported wounded as Russian strikes caused damage in 12 regions. Russia's bigger army hopes to exhaust Ukraine on the front line through sheer weight of numbers in terms of soldiers, armor and weapons. But Kyiv's defenses are largely holding the Russians back, sapping Russian momentum with the help of drones that quickly choke off troop advances. Russia has resorted to strategic bombing to wear down Ukraine's resistance, placing special emphasis on knocking out power ahead of winter, while Kyiv's domestically developed long-range drones and missiles have struck deep inside Russia, often targeting its oil refineries. In China, Trump called Putin "my friend." The American president's relationship with Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has soured. European leaders have tried to isolate Putin diplomatically and have heavily sanctioned the Russian economy. Ukrainian officials fear their country's fate could be determined by agreements between Trump and Putin, while European governments are alarmed by Moscow's aggression. The question of U.S. support for Ukraine, severely curtailed under Trump, could be raised by Democrats in Congress after their wins in the midterm elections. Britain's Prince Harry offered a veiled criticism of the U.S. government's policy toward Ukraine, saying in an interview released late Wednesday that he believes there is a "big separation" between the Trump administration's stance and that of the American people. Kushner and Witkoff have led Trump administration efforts to end nearly five years of war following Russia's all-out invasion of its neighbor and recently have mediated new discussions, though the talks have yielded no major breakthrough. Kushner said Thursday on X that Washington's priority at Thursday's meeting in Berlin is to "further strengthen our close coordination with Ukraine and Europe, work toward a unified position on the key elements of a lasting peace, and to jointly prepare the agenda and proposed format for the next round of multilateral negotiations." The meeting will also explore how Ukraine's European backers can fit into postwar security arrangements. Kyiv wants to ensure that Russia doesn't invade again, while Moscow wants to keep the NATO military alliance away from its borders. Putin said in Shenzhen that the Kremlin is not against European participation in talks, but "we need to understand with what Europe will come to these negotiations." The Kremlin has proposed to European officials through diplomatic channels to come to Moscow "to determine their position," Putin said, without elaborating. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov declined to say which European officials had been invited or whether Moscow had received a response, Russian state news agency Tass reported.

Price tag for US war in Iran barrels past $48 billion
articles.summary: A Pentagon budget officer has said the price of the Iran war surpassed $48.3 billion last week
articles.body: The cost of the US war in Iran , which Donald Trump launched without Congressional approval on February 28, blew past $48.3 billion (€44 billion) on November 13, according to Pentagon budgetary official Arthur Miller. Miller laid out the figures during Thursday testimony before the US Senate Armed Services Committee as his nomination to become Navy comptroller is considered. Miller said the costs cover US military operations, equipment and munitions but not damage sustained at US military installations across the Middle East. According to news agency AP, damage to hundreds of aircraft hangars, barracks, radar systems, warehouses and other US military infrastructure has run up into the billions of dollars, however, Miller failed to provide an estimate of the total cost when pressed during the hearing. Committee Chairman Roger Wicker, a Republican from Mississippi, called on Miller to provide the figures as soon as possible. In October, the Wall Street Journal cited Pentagon sources who said damage to US facilities in the region could range from $5 billion to as much as $15 billion. The Washington-based think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies put the cost for repairing buildings alone — excluding equipment and systems inside — at more than $4 billion. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The Trump administration has variously argued that the war is not a war, that it has been won, and that it will be over soon. There is currently no end in sight and on top of the US military's costs, the global economy is getting pummeled every day as a result of the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz — which is the direct result of US attacks on the Islamic Republic. The Trump administration is calling on Congress to pass the Pentagon's $1.5 trillion 2027 defense budget — a 40% increase over 2026 — in order to fund America's military. Unlikely prior to the November 3 midterm elections, the prospects of that figure being approved now that Democrats have taken control of both houses of Congress from Republicans would seem nigh impossible. Russian President Vladimir Putin arrives in Tajikistan for talks with Emomali Rahmon
articles.summary: Tajik President Emomali Rahmon welcomed his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, at Dushanbe International Airport
articles.body: Russian President Vladimir Putin has arrived in Tajikistan on a working visit, during which he is expected to discuss bilateral cooperation, regional security and developments in Afghanistan with President Emomali Rahmon, according to the Tajik president’s official website. Tajik President Emomali Rahmon welcomed his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, at Dushanbe International Airport. During the working visit, the two leaders are expected to discuss a range of issues of mutual interest, with a particular focus on strengthening cooperation between Tajikistan and Russia. According to Russia’s TASS news agency, Putin was invited by Rahmon, who visited Moscow last week to attend a summit of the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO). Putin reportedly explained that the two presidents had been unable to discuss all important bilateral issues during Rahmon’s visit because of their busy schedules. The leaders are now expected to discuss developments in Afghanistan, which was recently visited by a Russian delegation led by Deputy Prime Minister Alexey Overchuk. According to TASS , Putin will brief Rahmon on the prospects for expanding cooperation on Afghanistan-related issues. Another key item on the bilateral agenda is the operation of Russia’s 201st military base in Tajikistan, which Putin has previously described as a major guarantor of security across Central Asia. The two presidents will also discuss the development of bilateral relations, expanding economic ties between Moscow and Dushanbe, and promising joint projects, TASS reported. Putin last visited the Tajik capital in autumn 2025, when he paid a three-day state visit to the country. Putin’s visit comes amid renewed scrutiny of Tajikistan’s relationship with Russia, particularly following Dushanbe’s decision to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC). In October 2026, the Majlisi Namoyandagon, the lower house of Tajikistan’s parliament, approved the country’s withdrawal from the ICC. The withdrawal will take effect one year after formal notification is submitted to the UN secretary-general. According to Human Rights Watch (HRW), several countries have urged Tajikistan to reconsider its decision. In March 2026, ICC judges found that Tajikistan, as a state party to the Rome Statute, had failed to fulfill its obligation to arrest and surrender Russian President Vladimir Putin during his visit in October 2025. The court referred the matter to the Assembly of States Parties for further consideration. The ICC issued an arrest warrant for Putin in March 2023 over alleged war crimes related to the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children from occupied areas of Ukraine to Russia. Despite the warrant, Tajik authorities did not arrest the Russian president when he visited Dushanbe in October 2025. The ICC subsequently ruled that Tajikistan had failed to comply with its obligations under the Rome Statute. Some analysts believe Tajikistan’s decision to withdraw from the ICC reflects Dushanbe’s continued willingness to accommodate Moscow’s interests. They view the move as an attempt to avoid a potential diplomatic confrontation with Russia, which remains one of Tajikistan’s most important strategic partners.

articles.title: Constitutional Court President expels Zaza Bibilashvili from courtroom
articles.summary: The President of the Constitutional Court, Revaz Nadaraia, expelled Zaza Bibilashvili, representative of the National Movement, from the courtroom
articles.body: The President of the Constitutional Court, Revaz Nadaraia, expelled Zaza Bibilashvili, representative of the National Movement, from the courtroom. He explained this decision by stating that Zaza Bibilashvili had interrupted the judge multiple times on previous days as well and, "despite numerous warnings, did not stop similar behavior today either." "Mr. Zaza cannot get out of... he wants to address the public. Let the public decide this case for you then..." the judge remarked, after which Zaza Bibilashvili replied that "this case concerns the public." Immediately following this remark, the judge made the decision to expel Zaza Bibilashvili from the court hearing. "Zaza Bibilashvili has interrupted me once again. He constantly disrupts order at the court hearing, and you are expelled, Mr. Zaza, from the courtroom. This is already crossing every line and going too far. When the court warns you once, twice, three, four times, ignores elements containing insults, and you still do the same thing... Mr. Zaza Bibilashvili did not join us here to legally enrich this process; he came for disruption and to attack the parties and the court," Revaz Nadaraia stated. "This is very logical and highlights your impartiality—you are acting as one of the parties. Every time, I was simply asking for an equal approach between the parties," Bibilashvili remarked, to which Nadaraia replied that there is "an absolutely equal approach" at the trial. "There is an absolutely equal approach. You are the one demanding inequality in your favor," Nadaraia stated.

Armenian Opposition Spurns Pashinian’s Resignation Offer Over Constitutional Referendum
articles.body: Representatives of the two opposition factions in parliament reiterated their refusal to back a new constitution they say is being pursued by the government at Baku’s behest, dismissing Pashinian’s pledge as a political trap. Speaking to reporters following a cabinet meeting today, Pashinian repeated a proposal he first unveiled in parliament a day earlier, urging opposition lawmakers to provide the votes needed to put a new draft constitution to a nationwide referendum. Under his terms, he would resign immediately if voters reject the text and decline to seek another term as prime minister in the next general elections if the draft constitution is approved and a peace treaty with Baku is signed and ratified. “I am giving them [the opposition] an unbeatable option, and regardless of the outcome of the referendum, I would be leaving,” Pashinian said. “In one case, having left the peace agenda unfinished, because it turns out that this agenda does not receive the people’s support, at least as presented by me; in the second option, having implemented it in this capacity until the next elections, I will not be a candidate for prime minister in the next elections.” Pashinian warned that rejecting the offer would spell a “political death” for the opposition. Pashinian’s ruling Civil Contract party, which won the June 7 parliamentary elections, lacks the two-thirds majority required in the National Assembly to call a constitutional referendum and needs the backing of at least six opposition deputies. Lawmakers from the two parliamentary opposition factions, Strong Armenia and Hayastan, flatly ruled out any cooperation, stating they do not trust the prime minister and will not vote for what they label “Aliyev’s constitution,” a reference to Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. “By not entering into a deal with Pashinian, we are bypassing the trap set by Pashinian,” Hayastan lawmaker Kristine Vardanian told reporters. “I cannot imagine a scenario in which Pashinian proposes a deal with the real intention of leaving power. Trusting Pashinian’s words would truly be foolish.” Vardanian added that rejecting the offer is not a missed opportunity to oust the prime minister, arguing that “the possibility of removing Pashinian exists everywhere there is no deal with him.” Tigran Abrahamian, secretary of the Strong Armenia faction, echoed that stance, insisting that Armenia’s current constitution is “not subject to bargaining” and that his faction has no trust in Pashinian’s words. Levon Zurabian, deputy chairman of the extra-parliamentary Armenian National Congress, one of dozen opposition groups that recently united to campaign against the constitutional overhaul, also dismissed the prime minister’s proposal, citing what he described as Pashinian’s record of broken promises and alleged fraud in the June 7 parliamentary elections. Writing on Facebook, Zurabian argued that Pashinian should resign first and allow a consensus interim prime minister and a mutually trusted Central Electoral Commission to oversee any vote. He also demanded the release of all arrested activists whom the opposition regards as political prisoners and insisted that any referendum be limited strictly to whether to remove the reference to Armenia’s 1990 Declaration of Independence, the core of the current dispute. The constitutional standoff is central to efforts to finalize a peace treaty between Yerevan and Baku. Although Pashinian and Aliyev initialed a peace agreement during U.S.-brokered talks in Washington in August 2025, Azerbaijan has refused to sign the formal treaty until Armenia changes its constitution. Baku argues that the preamble’s reference to the 1990 Declaration of Independence, which in turn cites a 1989 unification act with Nagorno-Karabakh, constitutes a territorial claim against Azerbaijan and needs to be removed before a peace deal can be signed. Three weeks ago, Pashinian had promised to present the opposition with an offer they “could not reject” alongside guarantees that Azerbaijan would sign the peace treaty and raise no new demands once a new constitution is adopted. Pressed during today’s press briefing by RFE/RL’s Armenian Service on whether he had obtained such guarantees from Aliyev during their meeting on the margins of the European Political Community summit in Dublin last week, Pashinian did not cite any concrete commitments from Baku. “I provide that guarantee primarily with my own political capital – my political credibility,” Pashinian said, adding that while he had discussed the matter with the Azerbaijani leader in Dublin and is working to build broader international understanding, he was putting his own political future on the line. Pashinian confirmed that the preliminary text of the new constitution will be published next week. During his November 19 press briefing, he also stated that he plans to address the nation in the coming days, noting that the speech has not yet been written and will be delivered at the most appropriate time – tailored to how the opposition responds or fails to respond to his proposal. The prime minister warned that if the opposition blocks the referendum in parliament, his government will portray them as an “obstacle to peace” and seek snap parliamentary elections. “We will head for snap elections with this perception [of the opposition], and my gut feeling is that the two current opposition factions will not make it into the next parliament,” Pashinian said.

Emails reveal how Trump allies pushed pardons for election deniers
articles.body: In the fall of 2025, Cleta Mitchell, a key lawyer in Donald Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election, contacted a justice department official with an urgent request. Criminal cases against people who signed certificates falsely claiming that Trump won the presidential election in their state – known widely as fake electors – were pending in Georgia , Michigan, Arizona, Nevada and Wisconsin. She knew the official, pardon attorney Ed Martin, was working on a memo outlining why those involved in the fake elector scheme should receive a presidential pardon. Mitchell, a key figure in the movement to sow doubt about US elections, wanted the justice department to move forward with the pardons immediately before any of the cases went to trial. “Time is of the essence,” she wrote . “If trials (and in the Michigan case, an appeal of the dismissal) are allowed to occur, the additional financial and emotional costs to these loyal Trump supporters will be enormous,” she added in the message, which was obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight via a Freedom of Information Act request, and provided to the Guardian. “It is essential that the pardons move forward as quickly as possible before trials are scheduled and before these defendants are subjected to further expense and mental anguish. Please let me know what else I can do to help get this done.” Martin’s response to Mitchell’s email was brief. “Thank you for this,” he wrote. “Very helpful.” While the president eventually did issue a blanket pardon to the fake electors weeks later, the pardon was largely symbolic and did not affect the state-level charges they faced. The email exchange offers insight into the machinations that took place behind the scenes as key players in the election denial movement shaped the administration’s efforts to relitigate the 2020 election won by Joe Biden and to absolve loyalists of wrongdoing. “While the pardons were federal, not for the ongoing state cases, the documents shed light on the extent to which Mitchell and other Trump allies were using their access to get President Trump to act. Protecting our democratic system requires ensuring that no one, regardless of political influence or proximity to power, is placed above the law,” said Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight. A person close to the pardon effort said Martin had been pressing and working on the issue for months. Mitchell did not respond to a request for comment. In Georgia, at the time, the criminal case against Trump and fake electors were pending before the prosecuting attorneys council after Fulton county district attorney Fani Willis was disqualified. Mitchell suggested that a federal pardon could get the case dismissed. Other states, including Georgia, a slate of Republican electors had met privately and signed a certificate claiming Trump was the winner of the presidential election. Republicans sought to have those certificates recognized during the counting of the vote on 6 January 2021 – an effort that was unsuccessful. “If the pardons are issued promptly, before a new prosecutor is appointed, the Council can move for dismissal of the only remaining charges in the case, being the charges against President Trump,” she wrote to Martin. The prosecutor who eventually took over the case dismissed the charges, though it was for reasons unrelated to the pardons Trump issued. Mitchell’s interest in the Georgia case was notable. She was on the telephone call when Trump put pressure on Georgia secretary of state Brad Raffensperger to find enough votes to overturn the election. A special purpose grand jury in Georgia recommended criminally charging Mitchell for her involvement in the effort to overturn the election in the state, though she ultimately was never charged. Mitchell is a key figure in the election denial movement that has spread since the 2020 election. She has helped organize a network of local activists who have spread false and misleading information about elections. She is also linked to organizations that have provided funding for groups that have spread misleading information about elections. In Martin, Mitchell had a powerful ally. Prior to joining the justice department, he participated in the effort to overturn the 2020 election, speaking at a rally in Washington on 5 January 2021. “What they’re stealing is not just an election. It’s our future, and it’s our republic,” he said during the speech. On January 6, he posted on X : “I’m at the Capitol right now. Abd [sic] I was at the POTUS speech earlier. Rowdy crowd but nothing out of hand. Ignore the #FakeNews.” Martin represented some of those charged for January 6, and served on the board of an organization that provided financial assistance to their families. Before being appointed pardon attorney, he served as the interim US attorney for the District of Columbia, a position from which he fired and demoted prosecutors who worked on January 6 cases. Writing about the Arizona case, Mitchell urged a pardon before a grand jury could file charges, saying it would “be optimum to stop the persecution of these defendants, which include two of Charlie Kirk’s top lieutenants at TPUSA [Turning Point USA]”. Kirk had been slain in Utah only weeks earlier. Summarizing the Michigan and Wisconsin cases, Mitchell wrote that a presidential pardon could save defendants further financial burden. “Some of them have already spent their retirement funds, mortgaged their homes to pay legal fees, and suffered significant emotional hardship over the past four years. Allowing a trial to proceed is simply unacceptable.” The US constitution gives the president broad power to pardon people convicted of federal crimes. But not state ones. Nonetheless, Mitchell has publicly advanced a novel legal argument that a federal pardon for the fake elector scheme could wipe out the state charges. “The U.S. Constitution created the presidential electors and the federal Electoral Count Act controls the proceedings by which the electors conduct their federal responsibilities,” she wrote in an op-ed in the Federalist in November 2025. “We can reach only one conclusion: These are not true state charges, these are not state actors, and the entire scheme to concoct some odd collection of purported violations of state law are a nullity.” Mitchell also publicly advocated for the pardons on X . The Oversight Project, a rightwing group, published a memo in November 2025 making similar arguments. Trump eventually did issue a blanket pardon for the fake electors on 10 November 2025, though those pardons didn’t legally affect the state-level cases. In Wisconsin, the criminal case against three architects of the fake elector scheme is still pending. The cases against fake electors in Arizona , Michigan and Nevada have stalled for reasons unrelated to the pardons. The day Trump issued the blanket pardons, Martin received an email congratulating him on the pardons. “It was a long project,” Martin wrote. “But I am glad we stuck the landing.”

articles.title: Member of BiH Presidency Denis Becirovic holds separate Meetings with Ambassadors of Austria and Sweden
articles.summary: These meetings took place on the occasion of the commencement of Bećirović’s new term in the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina
articles.body: Denis Bećirović, a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, held separate meetings with the Ambassador of the Republic of Austria to Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georg Diwald, and the Ambassador of the Kingdom of Sweden to Bosnia and Herzegovina, Helena Lagerlöf. These meetings took place on the occasion of the commencement of Bećirović’s new term in the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. During his conversation with Ambassador Diwald, Bećirović highlighted that Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Austria enjoy exceptionally good and friendly bilateral relations. He recalled the official visit of the President of the Republic of Austria, Alexander Van der Bellen, to Bosnia and Herzegovina in April 2026, which further reaffirmed the strong ties between the two nations. He expressed particular gratitude to the Republic of Austria for its continuous support regarding the country’s European and Euro-Atlantic path, as well as for its significant contribution to the preservation of peace and security through its participation in the EUFOR Althea mission. Ambassador Diwald conveyed congratulations from the President of the Republic of Austria, Alexander Van der Bellen, wishing Bećirović a successful term. The member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina emphasized that the Republic of Austria is one of the country’s most important economic partners and largest foreign investors. He underscored the importance of further enhancing trade and investment, particularly in the sectors of energy, industry, and infrastructure. He also pointed to the significant role played by the large Bosnian-Herzegovinian diaspora in the Republic of Austria, which serves as a strong link between the two friendly nations. During the meeting with Ambassador Lagerlöf, Bećirović highlighted that Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Kingdom of Sweden maintain friendly relations and an intensive political dialogue. He recalled his official visit to the Kingdom of Sweden in August 2024, which included a meeting with King Carl XVI Gustaf. He expressed gratitude to the Kingdom of Sweden for its consistent support for the country’s European and Euro-Atlantic integration. Bećirović specifically thanked the Kingdom of Sweden for its long-standing development cooperation and significant financial support for reform processes in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He emphasized that Swedish support for strengthening democratic institutions, the rule of law, and the independence of the judiciary represents an important contribution to the overall development of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its progress toward the EU and NATO. He also pointed to opportunities for enhancing economic cooperation, as well as the significance of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian diaspora in Sweden in fostering ties between the two nations. Ambassadors Diwald and Lagerlöf expressed their readiness to continue strengthening bilateral cooperation with Bosnia and Herzegovina. They underscored the importance of preserving peace and stability, as well as continuing support for reform processes, according to a statement from the Office of the BiH Presidency Member Denis Bećirović.

articles.title: UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries
articles.summary: Last week, five EU countries announced an agreement in principle with Rwanda to establish a migrant “return hub” there in 2027
articles.body: The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document. A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”. Until now, the Home Office has been seeking bilateral agreements with third countries allowing the removal of migrants, but with no obvious success. Last week, five EU countries – Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands – announced an agreement in principle with Rwanda to establish a migrant “return hub” there in 2027. Burnham hinted at possible cooperation with EU countries last week when he told reporters that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that [the five-country deal] with interest, learning from what went on in the past”. He said: “The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.” The UK has been fighting for deeper cooperation with the EU on migration, with the new deal on a “strategic dialogue” secured in the last two weeks by negotiators in Brussels. It is a key part of the UK-EU reset pact, which also covers a youth mobility scheme, tariffs on Chinese imports, food and drink exports to the EU and a wider restatement of commitment on defence and security. Informed sources confirmed this was the first time the UK and the EU had agreed to “open a dialogue on returns” after the launch of the bloc’s Channel action plan in June this year. Whitehall sources said the UK was now open to the possibility of sending rejected claimants to Rwanda – a recent pivot from the position under Keir Starmer’s government, which rejected the move. According to a draft of the joint agreement, negotiations over third-country hubs will be part of increased cooperation to tackle irregular migration. The document states: “The EU and UK … will establish a structured dialogue on migration covering in particular the joint activities under the Channel action plan, action against irregular migration and migrant smuggling networks, strategic communication and border management, upstream cooperation and engagement with third countries, returns to third countries, pull factors for irregular migrants and legal pathway.” In May, the UK and 45 other European countries signed an agreement that explicitly endorsed plans to send unwanted asylum seekers to third-country hubs. A political declaration from the 46 members of the Council of Europe , the body that oversees the European convention on human rights (ECHR), said states had an “undeniable sovereign right” to control their borders. It is understood that the UK has been seeking a deal with an unnamed third country, similar to the Italy-Albania agreement that allowed Rome to place detention centres in Albania. Albania has ruled out a bilateral agreement on a return hub with the UK. Previous discussions have reportedly centred on 11 countries: Armenia, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, Libya, Mauritania, Rwanda, Senegal, Tunisia, Uganda and Uzbekistan. Montenegro has denied reports that it is considering housing refused asylum seekers. Starmer scrapped a Tory plan to forcibly send small-boat arrivals to Rwanda where their asylum claims would have been processed. Before the election, the Conservative government had spent £700m on its Rwanda returns policy, which was meant to deter Channel crossings. The scheme hit legal and political obstacles from the start, with the UK supreme court eventually ruling it illegal. Under Burnham, the Home Office has refused to close down the possibility of sending asylum seekers to Rwanda. This week, when asked if the UK might ever send asylum seekers to Rwanda, a Home Office spokesperson said: “The UK, like other European countries, is exploring innovative approaches including returns hubs to tackle illegal migration.” The UK has been looking for years to strengthen cooperation with France and other EU member states to tackle small boats carrying asylum seekers across the Channel. But sources say it is only in recent months that there has been a change of mood in the EU, with member states realising that the intensity of criminal trafficking across the Channel is “proving [to be] a pull factor” to enter the EU. Those that fail to make it to British shores remain in the EU’s migrant support system. Responding to the planned cooperation on migrant hubs, Madeleine Sumption, the head of the Migration Observatory at Oxford University, said: “Its inclusion in the statement would confirm the now relatively widespread interest in ‘third country’ options.” In response, Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, said return hubs were likely to be difficult and costly to run. “Removing people to places they have never stepped foot will be difficult and distressing,” he said. “The last decade has shown that working with people to support their return to their countries is far more successful.” A Home Office spokesperson said: “While we are not part of this EU member state initiative, there is widespread international agreement on the need to have practical and workable solutions to deal with the global challenge of illegal migration. “We continue to explore innovative approaches, including returns hubs, to build on the 80,000 people with no right to be in the UK returned or deported since July 2024. We have consistently made clear that we support the principle of returns hubs.”

articles.title: Tajik leader, Putin discuss efforts to counter regional security threats
articles.body: DUSHANBE, November 20. /TASS/. Tajik President Emomali Rahmon discussed the regional situation and ways to counter threats and challenges with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, the Tajik leader’s press service said. During their talks, the two presidents discussed in detail "the situation in the region and efforts to address security challenges and threats such as terrorism, extremism, manifestations of radicalism, cyber threats and drug trafficking," the press service reported. Rahmon and Putin also praised coordination between the two countries’ authorities during the meeting. "The two heads of state praised how effectively their countries’ law enforcement agencies, security services and defense institutions work together," the statement said. Putin had earlier told reporters that he planned to discuss the situation surrounding Afghanistan and the operation of Russia’s 201st Military Base with his Tajik counterpart.

European security system overhaul only way to keep war at bay — Russian envoy
articles.summary: Unfortunately, the European security system lies in ruins, and the activity - or, more precisely, inactivity - of our organization
articles.body: VIENNA, November 20. /TASS/. War will eventually come to Europe unless the continent’s degraded security system is reformed, Russian Permanent Representative to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) Dmitry Polyansky said. "Unfortunately, the European security system lies in ruins, and the activity - or, more precisely, inactivity - of our organization, which is incapable of even discussing the issue like adults, is the best proof of that. The security architecture will have to be restored, taking into account the lessons learned over the past decades and the principles that were once enshrined in the OSCE’s founding documents, including the principle of equal and indivisible security preventing countries from strengthening their security at the expense of others. The only alternative to this - war," he pointed out at an OSCE Permanent Council meeting. The diplomat stressed that Moscow was ready to discuss security guarantees for all European countries, including Ukraine and Russia. "We have never cut off dialogue with Europe and have remained open to it. However, it takes two to build dialogue, and Europe should finally decide what it wants: peace or war," he concluded.

articles.title: Trump’s CISA nominee ducks questions on 2020 election results, Jan. 6 Capitol attack
articles.summary: LoSapio serves as the chief information security officer at tech company Palantir
articles.body: Michael LoSapio, President Trump's nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), on Thursday ducked questions from lawmakers about the Jan. 6, 2021, U.S. Capitol attack and who won the 2020 presidential election. LoSapio serves as the chief information security officer at tech company Palantir. He told Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), when asked for his thoughts about who won in 2020, that he was "not going to answer the question about an election six years ago," according to video of the exchange shared by Blumenthal on the social platform X. "You're supposed to look at the facts and you're supposed to tell us the facts," Blumenthal said. "I'm asking you a factual question." "My only involvement in the 2020 election was voting for the President of the United States," he added. Blumenthal accused him of avoiding the question, adding that this "betrays your lack of independence and objectivity," and again asked him to answer his question about who won the 2020 popular vote. "No sir, I'm here to talk to you about the future," LoSapio replied. "You're disqualified from the position that you've been nominated to fill," Blumenthal said. The Connecticut Democrat also asked LoSapio about the Jan. 6 attack, to which LoSapio replied that he did not believe it was an attack. "I wasn’t involved in politics," he said. "I know what I saw on the news." Politico reported that Sens. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) and Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) plan to place a hold on LoSapio's nomination. Punchbowl News reported that Tillis will block the confirmation due to LoSapio's comments about the Jan. 6 attack. Wyden told Politico that "you can't have an insurrectionist Palantir executive in charge of our nation's cybersecurity and elections security." Senate Homeland Security Chair Rand Paul (R-Ky.) said the vote to confirm LoSapio will be held in early December, the outlet reported. "It was big, it was huge and it shouldn’t be excused, it should be criticized,” Paul, a critic of the attack, said during the hearing. "It was some attack, some riot, but it was also some people, and some of these people got locked up … that weren’t violent." Other Trump nominees have similarly answered questions about Jan. 6, including Don R. Berthiaume, the nominee for Department of Justice inspector general. He said there was "violence on the Capitol grounds," but added that "I don't know if I would use the term attack," The Associated Press reported. The last head of CISA was Jen Easterly in January 2025. Trump had nominated former Energy Department and Coast Guard official Sean Plankey before he withdrew his nomination when it failed to pass the Senate. Near the end of his first term, Trump fired former CISA Director Chris Krebs after affirming that the 2020 election, where Trump lost reelection, was secure. The president has claimed that he won the 2020 election, though former President Biden won the Electoral College vote and served until 2025.

articles.title: Trump says he doesn’t need help from Russia, China to end Iran war
articles.summary: Well, you know, we don't need any help," Trump told Fox News's Jacqui Heinrich while in Shenzhen, China
articles.body: President Trump on Wednesday said he does not need Russia and China's help to conclude the Iran war, before meeting with the leaders of both countries for an unprecedented summit in China the following day. "Well, you know, we don't need any help," Trump told Fox News's Jacqui Heinrich while in Shenzhen, China. "We've defeated [Iran's] navy, we've defeated their air force, we've defeated their anti-aircraft. Their missiles are down to about 12 –– they still have some missiles, but they're down to about 12, 13 percent of what they were." "And they want to make a deal," he added. "So, I don't need help. I mean, I'm not going to go and ask them for help." Trump said Iran has treated the U.S. "very well" and that they "haven't fired, they haven't put ships in the water." The president did not acknowledge the Iranian strikes on a U.S. air base in Kuwait on Wednesday or multiple one-way drone attacks on a U.S. radar facility in Bahrain on Tuesday, following similar strikes — including a U.S. strike on Qeshm Island — late last week. Iran has ramped up its attacks on U.S. targets and allies in the region after both sides have largely held off on retaliatory strikes since September. Washington and Tehran have sought a diplomatic end to the war, which began on Feb. 28. Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a historic 90-minute trilateral meeting. All three leaders released a four-point "peace declaration" calling for promoting reforms at the United Nations "so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges." The declaration added "that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction" and reaffirmed that a nuclear war must never be fought. The leaders also said they intend to "increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations." Trump told reporters before the summit that he wanted to discuss the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war with Xi and Putin. China and Russia have both supported Iran by buying its oil, reportedly providing intelligence and maintaining trade ties to help Tehran resist U.S. military and economic pressure. Both countries have denied aiding Iran in its fight against the U.S. Trump received a boost of support from some Republican lawmakers back home, but others hope the president knows that, as Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) said, "China and Russia are not our friends, though." Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.), who will be leaving the Senate in January for Alabama's governor's mansion, previously told The Hill that he did not care who Trump is meeting with, "we've got to get this over with," referring to the wars in Ukraine and Iran. "They’re all involved in some form or fashion," Tuberville said. "So you bring all the leaders of the world together and try to work it out. I mean, I’d rather him do that than sit over here and worry about air traffic control."

Russia has no plans to attack NATO members — Foreign Ministry
articles.summary: Moscow seeks to live in peace and has no plans to attack NATO countries, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said
articles.body: MOSCOW, November 20. /TASS/. Moscow seeks to live in peace and has no plans to attack NATO countries, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said. "Russia has no intention of attacking NATO member states, something they fantasize about so openly and with a kind of maniacal perversity," she stated at a briefing. "We want to live in peace and harmony with our neighbors and with all countries," the diplomat emphasized. That is why Moscow "has repeatedly proposed various initiatives to ease military and political tensions specifically in Europe, suggested reaching agreement on mutual security guarantees, and done so in writing on multiple occasions in recent history," Zakharova said. "We hope all of this reaches those who make decisions or plan strategy, and that it is heard by political forces in Western countries that take the well-being of their own citizens seriously and regard it as an imperative," she concluded.

Trilateral talks in Shenzhen confirmed Russia’s status — Bloomberg
articles.summary: In his view, the meeting "in itself was a major triumph for [Russian President Vladimir] Putin
articles.body: NEW YORK, November 20. /TASS/. The trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China and the United States on the sidelines of the APEC summit symbolized the failure of Western efforts to isolate Russia and marked a triumph for the Russian leader, Bloomberg columnist Marc Champion wrote. In his view, the meeting "in itself was a major triumph for [Russian President Vladimir] Putin." "It affirms his country’s status, symbolizes the defeat of Western efforts to isolate Russia and belittles his richer rivals in Europe," Champion wrote. The columnist believes that the Russian leader "can reasonably hope that this great-power troika will surely meet again." Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and US President Donald Trump held a meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, the first such meeting ever. The heads of state exchanged views on the current international situation and expressed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security. The leaders also adopted a declaration on peace. They expressed support for reforming the UN to ensure a more effective response to the global challenges. According to the document, Russia, China, and the United States plan to increase the production and supply of petroleum products for the benefit of all countries. It is noted that respect for the immunities of state officials is of fundamental importance, and the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies should not abuse their powers. The leaders emphasized that a nuclear war must never be unleashed - there will be no winners in it. It is also noted that Russia, China, and the United States will engage in dialogue to reduce nuclear risks.
